title: Advanced Client Management: Keeping and Growing High-Value Clients
subtitle: Run your most valuable client accounts with clear agreements, early warning signs, honest reviews and well-planned renewals.
description: This course is for women who already serve paying clients and now need to keep and grow the important ones. You will measure how much your business depends on each client, set up onboarding and retainer controls, run quarterly reviews, handle failures honestly and plan renewals. You finish with a Client Relationship Management Playbook you can use with every major account.
outcomes: Calculate each client's share of your income and sort accounts into strategic, key and standard tiers
Build and use a weighted account health score to spot weakening relationships early
Onboard a new account with a kickoff agenda, communication charter and RACI chart
Track retainer hours, handle change requests in writing and run a quarterly business review
Lead a service recovery conversation and plan a renewal with a justified price adjustment
Hand over an account safely and document a relationship challenge with honest reflection
audience: Freelancers, agency and small business owners, and account or client success staff who already manage regular paying clients and want to keep and grow their most valuable ones.
tools: A smartphone or computer with WhatsApp and email
A spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel (free mobile versions work)
A notebook or notes app for your client records
Your own list of current clients and what they pay

modules.title: Foundations: Value, Trust and Account Health
modules.overview: High-value clients behave differently from one-off customers, and they carry different risks. In this module you measure how much your business depends on each client, learn a practical model of trust, and build a simple health score that warns you before a good account goes quiet.

lessons.title: High-value accounts: concentration risk and account tiers
objectives: Calculate what share of your monthly income each client provides
Explain concentration risk and what happens to your business if a large client leaves
Sort your clients into strategic, key and standard tiers
Decide how much time and attention each tier should receive

blocks.text: Most client advice is written for the first sale. This course is about what happens after. A **high-value account** is a client who pays you regularly, often on a monthly **retainer** (a fixed fee for an agreed amount of ongoing work), and whose loss would hurt your income. A social media manager with a monthly hospital contract, a bookkeeper serving three schools, or a caterer who supplies an office canteen every week all manage accounts like this.

Advanced client management has three jobs. First, **keep** the account by delivering reliably and communicating well. Second, **protect** it by spotting trouble early. Third, **grow** it through renewal at a fair price and, where it truly helps the client, extra work. Before any of that, you need to know which clients matter most to your business, in numbers, not feelings.

blocks.name: investment-data
blocks.alt: A woman studying charts that show money coming in
blocks.caption: Start by looking at where your monthly income actually comes from, client by client.

blocks.text: Concentration risk

**Concentration risk** is the danger of depending on one or two clients for a large share of your income. A big client feels like good news, and it is, until that client changes manager, cuts budget or moves the work in-house. If one account pays most of your bills, losing it can force you to lay off staff or borrow. The cure is not to avoid big clients. It is to know your exposure, manage that account with extra care, and keep building other income so no single exit can sink you.

blocks.title: Worked example: one agency's exposure
blocks.context: For example, Ada runs a three-person digital marketing agency in Lagos with five retainer clients. Her monthly team and office costs are about N900,000. These are example figures for practice, not market prices.
steps: She lists monthly fees: Client A N600,000, Client B N250,000, Client C N200,000, Client D N150,000, Client E N100,000.
She works out Client A's share: 600,000 divided by 1,300,000 = 0.46, so about 46% of her income.
She tests the worst case: without Client A, income falls to 1,300,000 minus 600,000 = N700,000, which is N200,000 below her N900,000 costs every month.
She works out Client A's yearly value: 600,000 x 12 = N7,200,000.
blocks.result: Ada now knows that one client carries nearly half her business. She decides to give Client A her most senior attention, set her own limit that no single client should exceed about a third of income, and spend two hours a week winning new work so that share falls over time.

blocks.text: Sorting clients into tiers

Not every client needs the same level of service. Giving everyone the same attention usually means your best clients get too little and your smallest get more than they pay for. A simple three-tier system helps you decide where your hours go. Use your own business numbers to set the boundaries.

head: Tier
Typical signs
Attention you give
rows: Strategic
Large share of income, long contract, room to grow, senior contact
Owner or most senior person leads; monthly check-in; quarterly review; health score every month
Key
Steady monthly fee, good fit, some growth possible
Named account lead; fortnightly update; review twice a year
Standard
Small or occasional work, clear and simple scope
Efficient service, templates, update at each delivery

blocks.title: Account tiers
blocks.caption: Few accounts sit at the top, but they deserve the most senior time and the closest watching.

blocks.text: Tiers are about service level, not respect. A standard client still deserves courtesy, honesty and on-time delivery. The difference is in how much proactive time you invest, such as strategy calls, reviews and extra ideas. Review tiers every quarter, because a standard client can grow into a key one, and a strategic one can shrink.

blocks.title: Do not let one client run your business
blocks.text: When a client knows they are most of your income, the pressure to say yes to everything grows: unpaid extras, late-night calls, delayed payments. Knowing your exposure helps you stay calm and professional, because you are already working on a plan B.
Where this skill is used

In companies, this work is called account management or client success. In agencies and consulting firms, a named account lead owns each large client. Freelancers and small business owners do the same job themselves. Remote clients, including clients abroad who pay through platforms or in foreign currency, need even more deliberate management, because you rarely meet in person and silence is easy to misread.

items: Keep: deliver what you promised, on time, and say so clearly.
Protect: watch for warning signs and act before the client complains.
Grow: renew on fair terms and offer extra work only when it serves the client's goals.

takeaways: A high-value account is one whose loss would seriously hurt your income.
Work out each client's share of income; a single client near half your income is a serious risk.
Sort clients into strategic, key and standard tiers and match your time to the tier.
Reduce concentration risk by managing the big account carefully and steadily adding other clients.

activity.title: Map your income exposure
steps: List every client who paid you in the last three months and their average monthly payment.
Add the total and calculate each client's percentage share (client amount divided by total, times 100).
Write down what would happen to your monthly income if your largest client left.
Place each client in the strategic, key or standard tier and note one change in how you will serve your top client.
activity.evidence: A one-page table or spreadsheet showing clients, monthly amounts, percentage shares and tiers

lessons.title: How trust is built: the Trust Equation and multi-threaded relationships
objectives: Name the four parts of the Trust Equation and what each one means
Score your own trustworthiness with a client and find the weakest part
Plan specific actions that raise reliability and lower self-orientation
Build relationships with more than one person inside a client organisation

blocks.text: Clients rarely leave because of one mistake. They leave when they stop trusting you. Trust can feel mysterious, but it can be broken down into parts you can work on. A useful model is the **Trust Equation**, first published in the book *The Trusted Advisor* (2000), co-written by David Maister, Charles H. Green and Robert Galford.
The four parts

head: Part
Question it answers
What it looks like with a client
rows: Credibility
Can I believe what you say?
You know your field, give accurate answers and admit when you do not know
Reliability
Do you do what you said?
Reports arrive on the agreed day; you return calls when you said you would
Intimacy
Do I feel safe telling you things?
The client shares worries and bad news with you because you keep confidences and do not judge
Self-orientation
Whose interests are you focused on?
High when you push your own sales or talk about yourself; low when you listen and focus on the client's goals

blocks.text: The equation puts credibility, reliability and intimacy on top, added together, and self-orientation underneath. In words: **trust grows when the top three rise and falls when self-orientation rises.** Self-orientation is the one most people overlook. You can be skilled and punctual, but if the client senses you care more about the next invoice than about their results, trust drops.

blocks.name: handshake-deal
blocks.alt: Two professionals shaking hands across a table
blocks.caption: A signed contract starts the relationship; trust is what keeps it going.

blocks.title: Worked example: scoring and fixing trust
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi is a bookkeeper who serves a private school in Abuja on a monthly retainer. The bursar has gone quiet. Ngozi does an honest self-check, giving each part a score from 1 (weak) to 10 (strong). This is a personal reflection tool, not an official test.
steps: She scores herself: Credibility 7, Reliability 4 (two monthly reports were late), Intimacy 6, Self-orientation 5 (her last two calls were about adding payroll services).
She adds the top three: 7 + 4 + 6 = 17. She divides by self-orientation: 17 divided by 5 = 3.4.
Her weakest areas are clear: reliability, and too much selling.
She commits to sending reports on the 5th of every month and stops pitching new services until the school raises a need.
Three months later she rescores: Reliability 8, Self-orientation 3. The top three now add to 7 + 8 + 6 = 21, and 21 divided by 3 = 7.0.
blocks.result: The number itself is only a guide, but the exercise showed Ngozi exactly what to fix. Being on time and focusing on the school's problems did more for trust than any new service offer.

blocks.title: Self-oriented or client-oriented?
blocks.caption: Moving habits from the left column to the right lowers self-orientation, the denominator of the Trust Equation.

blocks.text: Practical ways to raise each part

items: Credibility: check facts before you send them, and say 'Let me confirm and come back to you by 3pm' instead of guessing.
Reliability: make small promises and keep them every time. Missed small promises add up faster than people expect.
Intimacy: keep what clients tell you private, remember what matters to them, and respond to bad news without blame.
Self-orientation: in every call, spend more time asking and listening than talking about yourself.

blocks.text: Do not rely on one contact

Many accounts are lost because the one person who liked you leaves the company. A **multi-threaded** relationship means you have good working links with several people at the client: the person who approves payment, the person you work with every day, and ideally someone senior who cares about the results. You build these links honestly, by copying the right people on reports they actually need, inviting the sponsor to quarterly reviews, and thanking colleagues who help.
Trust signals in remote relationships

With clients you rarely meet, such as a company in another state or abroad, trust is built almost entirely through small written and spoken signals. Answer within the time you agreed, even if only to say 'Received, I will reply fully by Thursday.' Turn on your camera for important video calls so the client sees a real person. Write updates that are short, specific and dated, so the client never has to chase you. When you are unsure of a time zone or a public holiday, ask, rather than assume.

items: Confirm every request in writing, even briefly.
Send bad news before the client finds it.
Use the client's name and refer to what they told you last time.
Keep personal opinions on politics and religion out of business chats.

blocks.title: Respect the main contact
blocks.text: Never go around your day-to-day contact to complain to their boss. Agree with your contact who should receive which updates, so wider relationships strengthen their position rather than threaten it.

takeaways: Trust has four parts: credibility, reliability, intimacy and self-orientation.
High self-orientation, such as constant selling, can cancel out strong skills.
Small, kept promises are the fastest way to rebuild reliability.
Build honest working links with several people at each important client.

activity.title: Your trust self-check
steps: Choose one important client and score yourself from 1 to 10 on each of the four parts.
Calculate (credibility + reliability + intimacy) divided by self-orientation.
Write the evidence for your lowest score, such as dates of late deliveries.
List two actions for the next 30 days that will improve that weakest part.
Name everyone you know at this client and mark who you have not spoken to in two months.
activity.evidence: A short note with your four scores, the calculation, two dated actions and your contact list for that client

lessons.title: Building an account health score that warns you early
objectives: List warning signs that a client relationship is weakening
Build a weighted health score from five signals
Calculate a score and place an account in a green, amber or red band
Choose the right action for each band

blocks.text: By the time a client says 'We have decided not to renew', the decision was usually made weeks earlier. The signs were there: slower replies, a new manager who never joined a call, invoices paid later than before. An **account health score** collects those signs into one number so you notice the pattern while there is still time to act.
Warning signs to watch

head: Signal
Healthy
Warning
rows: Your delivery
Work arrives on time and needs few corrections
Missed dates, repeated revisions
Client responsiveness
Approvals and feedback come within the agreed time
Messages left on 'read', approvals delayed for days
Satisfaction
Positive feedback, client asks for your opinion
Complaints, short or cold replies, no feedback at all
Payment behaviour
Invoices paid on the due date
Payments later each month, requests for discounts
Sponsor engagement
The decision-maker attends reviews and knows your results
Sponsor has changed or never appears

blocks.name: business-analytics
blocks.alt: A person reviewing a dashboard of charts and scores
blocks.caption: A health score turns scattered signs into one figure you can watch month by month.

blocks.text: Building a weighted score

Score each signal from 1 (very poor) to 5 (excellent) once a month. Because some signals matter more than others, give each one a **weight**, a percentage that shows its importance. The weights must add up to 100%. The weights below are a sensible starting point; adjust them to your business. Then multiply each score by its weight and add the results. The final number is out of 5.

items: Agree your weights, for example: delivery 25%, responsiveness 15%, satisfaction 25%, payment 20%, sponsor engagement 15%.
Score each signal from 1 to 5 using facts from the month, not your mood.
Multiply each score by its weight written as a decimal (25% is 0.25).
Add the five results to get a score out of 5.
Place the account in a band and take the matching action.

blocks.title: Worked example: scoring two accounts
blocks.context: For example, Ada from Lesson 1 scores two of her clients at the end of the month using the weights above.
steps: Client A scores: delivery 4, responsiveness 3, satisfaction 2 (two complaints about post quality), payment 5, sponsor engagement 2 (new marketing director has not met Ada).
Client B scores: delivery 5, responsiveness 4, satisfaction 4, payment 3, sponsor 4.
blocks.result: Client B is green. Client A, her largest account, is amber at 3.25, even though it pays on time. Ada books a meeting with the new marketing director within two weeks and agrees a quality check on posts before they go out.

blocks.title: Monthly health check routine
blocks.caption: Repeat the same routine every month so changes in the score mean something.

head: Band (example cut-offs)
Score
Action
rows: Green
Keep the rhythm; look for renewal and growth ideas
Amber
Find the weakest signal; agree a fix with the client within two weeks
Red
Below 3.0
Owner or senior lead calls the sponsor; written recovery plan; weekly follow-up

blocks.title: Watch the trend, not just the number
blocks.text: A score that drops from 4.4 to 3.6 over three months is more worrying than a steady 3.6. Keep a monthly history so you can see the direction.
Ask the client directly

Your score is your view. Balance it with the client's own view by asking one short question each month, at the end of your monthly report: 'On a scale of 1 to 5, how satisfied are you with our work this month, and what is one thing we could do better?' Use the answer as the satisfaction score. A client who gives a 3 and names a specific problem is giving you a gift: a clear thing to fix while the account is still yours. A client who stops answering this question is also telling you something, so lower the responsiveness score and pick up the phone.

Keep the score honest. If you score yourself kindly on delivery, the tool becomes useless. Use evidence: dates in your project tracker, payment dates from your bank or Moniepoint, Opay or Paystack records, and the client's own words in emails or WhatsApp messages. When you store these notes, remember they are about real people and businesses. Keep them in a password-protected file and do not share them outside your team.

takeaways: Lost accounts usually show warning signs weeks before the client says so.
A weighted score from five signals gives one comparable number each month.
Weights must add to 100%; multiply each score by its weight and add.
Use bands to decide actions, and watch the direction of the score over time.

activity.title: Score your top three accounts
steps: Copy the five signals and weights into a spreadsheet or notebook.
Score your three most valuable clients for last month, writing one fact beside each score.
Calculate each weighted total and place each account in a band.
For any amber or red account, write one action with a date and the name of the person you will contact.
activity.evidence: Your health score sheet for three clients with totals, bands and dated actions

quiz.q: Funmi's clients pay N400,000, N300,000, N200,000 and N100,000 a month. What share of her income comes from her largest client?
quiz.explain: Total income is N1,000,000. 400,000 divided by 1,000,000 = 0.40, which is 40%.

quiz.q: In the Trust Equation, which change would most likely raise trust when a consultant's skills are already strong?
options: Talking more about her past achievements
Offering a new service in every meeting
Reducing self-orientation by listening more and selling less
quiz.explain: Self-orientation sits underneath the equation. Lowering it, by focusing on the client rather than on yourself, raises trust.

quiz.q: A client's health scores are delivery 3, responsiveness 4, satisfaction 3, payment 4, sponsor 2, with weights 25%, 15%, 25%, 20%, 15%. What is the total?
quiz.explain: 0.75 + 0.60 + 0.75 + 0.80 + 0.30 = 3.20 out of 5, which falls in the amber band.

quiz.q: Kemi's only contact at a large client has just resigned. Which earlier habit would have protected the account best?
options: Building working links with the sponsor and other team members
Using more emojis in WhatsApp updates
quiz.explain: A multi-threaded relationship means the account does not depend on one person, so a resignation is less likely to end it.

quiz.q: Which client should normally receive a monthly check-in and a quarterly review led by the most senior person?
options: A standard client who orders twice a year
A strategic client with a large share of income and room to grow
quiz.explain: Strategic accounts carry the most value and risk, so they get the most senior and most regular attention.

quiz.q: An account's health score has fallen from 4.3 to 3.5 over three months. What is the best next step?
options: Wait to see if it improves
Find the weakest signal and agree a fix with the client within two weeks
Reduce the client's tier to standard
quiz.explain: A falling trend into amber calls for finding the cause and acting quickly, before it becomes red.

modules.title: Onboarding, Retainer Control and Quarterly Reviews
modules.overview: Most problems with large clients start in the first month or creep in through unmanaged extra requests. This module gives you an onboarding kit with a communication charter and RACI chart, a method for tracking retainer hours and handling change requests, and a quarterly business review that shows the client the value they receive.

lessons.title: The onboarding kit: kickoff meeting, communication charter and RACI
objectives: Plan the first 30 days of a new high-value account
Run a kickoff meeting with a clear agenda
Write a communication charter covering channels, response times and escalation
Build a RACI chart so both sides know who does and decides what

blocks.text: The first month of a new account sets habits that last for years. If the client learns that you answer WhatsApp at 11pm, they will expect it. If nobody agrees who approves work, you will wait days for decisions and get blamed for delays. **Onboarding** is the planned process of starting a client relationship so that expectations are written down and agreed before the pressure of real deadlines begins.

blocks.name: onboarding
blocks.alt: A person being guided through the first steps of a new process
blocks.caption: A planned onboarding turns a signed contract into a working relationship with clear rules.

blocks.text: The first 30 days

blocks.title: First 30 days of a new account
blocks.caption: Each stage has one job, ending with a review where both sides say what is and is not working.

blocks.text: The kickoff meeting

Hold a kickoff call or meeting within three working days of signing, with the main contact and, if possible, the sponsor who approved the budget. Send the agenda a day before. Cover: the client's goals for the next three to twelve months and how they will judge success; the agreed scope from the contract, read aloud in plain words; who is involved on both sides; how you will communicate; what you need from them (logins, brand files, data) and by when; and the date of the first delivery. Send written notes the same day and ask the client to confirm or correct them.
The communication charter

A **communication charter** is a short, agreed document that sets the rules for how you and the client talk. It protects both sides: the client knows when to expect answers, and you protect your evenings and weekends. Keep it to one page.

head: Item
Example wording
rows: Channels
WhatsApp group for quick questions; email for approvals, invoices and anything that changes scope
Response times
Replies within 4 working hours, Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm; urgent issues by phone call
Regular updates
Written progress update every Friday by 3pm; monthly report by the 5th
Approvals
Client approves or comments within 2 working days; after that, the schedule moves
Escalation
If a problem is not solved by the account lead in 2 working days, it goes to the agency owner and the client's marketing manager

blocks.text: The RACI chart

Confusion about roles causes many client disputes. A **RACI chart** lists each recurring task and marks who is **R**esponsible (does the work), **A**ccountable (owns the result and makes the final decision), **C**onsulted (gives input before) and **I**nformed (is told after). Common guidance is to have exactly one Accountable person per task, so there is always one clear decision-maker.

blocks.title: Worked example: a RACI chart for a hospital social media retainer
blocks.context: For example, Ada's agency starts managing Facebook and Instagram for a private hospital in Ibadan. On the agency side are Ada (owner) and Tolu (content writer). On the client side are Bisi (marketing officer) and the medical director.
steps: Monthly content calendar: Tolu is R, Ada is A, Bisi is C, the medical director is I.
Approval of any post with health information: Bisi is R, the medical director is A, Ada is C, Tolu is I.
Publishing approved posts: Tolu is R, Ada is A, Bisi is I.
Replying to patient comments: Bisi is R and A because only hospital staff may discuss patient matters; Ada is C on tone; Tolu is I.
Ada checks every row has exactly one A, then shares the chart at the kickoff for agreement.
blocks.result: Both teams now know that the medical director, not the agency, signs off health information, and that the hospital handles patient questions. This protects patients, the hospital and Ada's agency from a serious mistake.

blocks.title: Access and client data
blocks.text: Never ask for a client's personal passwords. Ask to be added with your own login or partner access, which most business platforms provide, so access can be removed when the work ends. Keep client and customer data private and use it only for the agreed work. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, sets rules for handling personal data.
The client inputs list

Many first deliveries are late because the provider is waiting for things from the client. At kickoff, agree a written list of inputs with an owner and a due date for each: logo and brand colours, product price list, access to the social media pages, previous reports, and the names of anyone who must approve work. Track the list in your weekly update. If an input is late, say so politely and show the effect on the schedule, so a delay is never blamed on you by default.

items: Send the charter and RACI with the kickoff notes and ask for written agreement.
Pin the charter in the WhatsApp group so new members see it.
At the Day 30 review, ask: what should we start, stop or keep doing?

takeaways: Agree expectations in writing before real deadlines start.
A kickoff meeting covers goals, scope, people, communication, client inputs and the first delivery date.
A one-page communication charter sets channels, response times, update days and escalation.
A RACI chart names one accountable person per task and prevents blame later.

activity.title: Build your onboarding kit
steps: Choose a current or likely high-value client.
Write a kickoff agenda with the six items from this lesson.
Draft a one-page communication charter using the five rows in the table.
List four recurring tasks and complete a RACI chart, checking there is one A per task.
activity.evidence: Your kickoff agenda, communication charter and RACI chart saved as one document

lessons.title: Retainer control: tracking hours, preventing scope creep and change requests
objectives: Calculate the effective hourly rate of a retainer
Track hours used against hours included and project the month-end total
Tell the difference between in-scope work and a change request
Handle a change request in writing with an estimate and clear choices

blocks.text: A **retainer** is a fixed monthly fee for an agreed amount of ongoing work, such as 30 hours of marketing support or 12 social media posts. Retainers are good for both sides: the client gets steady service, and you get predictable income. They also carry a quiet danger: **scope creep**, where small extra requests pile up until you are doing far more work for the same fee. Scope creep rarely comes from bad clients. It comes from unclear scope and nobody tracking the hours.

blocks.name: schedule
blocks.alt: A person organising tasks on a large schedule board
blocks.caption: Tracking hours against the retainer every week shows trouble before the month is over.

blocks.text: Know your effective rate

Divide the monthly fee by the hours included to get your **effective hourly rate**. This is the number you use to price extra work and to see whether an account is profitable. If you regularly work more hours than included, your real rate falls without anyone noticing.

blocks.title: Worked example: a month that is running over
blocks.context: For example, Halima's agency has a retainer with a school: N450,000 a month for 30 hours of marketing work. These are example figures. It is day 15 of a 30-day month and her time log shows 21 hours used.
steps: Effective rate: 450,000 divided by 30 hours = N15,000 per hour.
Hours used so far: 21 out of 30, which is 70% of the hours with only 50% of the month gone.
Projected month total: 21 hours divided by 15 days, times 30 days = 42 hours.
Projected overrun: 42 minus 30 = 12 hours. At N15,000 per hour, that is 12 x 15,000 = N180,000 of unpaid work.
She checks the log: 9 of the 21 hours went on a new admissions landing page that was never in the scope.
blocks.result: Halima now has facts, not a feeling. She treats the landing page as a change request, and she shares the hours summary with the school before the overrun happens, not after.

blocks.text: In scope or a change request?

head: In scope (part of the retainer)
Change request (extra, needs approval)
rows: Work listed in the contract, such as 12 posts a month
New deliverables, such as a website page or a video
Normal revisions agreed in the contract, such as two rounds
A fourth or fifth round of revisions after approval
Monthly report in the agreed format
A new report for the board in a different format
Work within agreed hours
Rush work outside agreed working hours

blocks.title: Handling a change request
blocks.caption: Every extra request follows the same path, so nothing is done for free by accident.

blocks.text: Giving the client choices

Do not answer an extra request with a flat 'no' or a silent 'yes'. Thank the client, estimate the work and offer clear options. For the landing page, Halima estimates 10 hours. She writes by email: 'Thank you for the landing page request. It is outside our monthly scope. We estimate 10 hours, which is N150,000 at our retainer rate. You can: (1) approve it as extra work, invoiced separately; (2) swap it for 10 hours of this month's planned work, which would move the March newsletter to April; or (3) schedule it for next month within the normal hours.' The client chooses, and the choice is recorded.

items: Log time daily against each client and task, using a simple sheet or a free time-tracking app.
Every Friday, compare hours used with hours included and project the month-end total.
At 75% of hours used, tell the client and agree priorities for the rest of the month.
Send a short monthly hours summary with the report so the client sees what the fee bought.

blocks.text: Write scope so it can be measured

Most scope creep starts with vague words in the agreement, such as 'social media support' or 'reasonable revisions'. Replace them with countable terms: '12 posts per month across Facebook and Instagram', 'up to two rounds of revisions per post', 'replies within 4 working hours, Monday to Friday', 'work requested after 5pm on Friday starts on Monday'. Also list what is not included, for example paid advertising budgets, printing or photography. Clear scope does not make you rigid. It gives you and the client a shared reference point, so a conversation about extra work feels fair rather than personal.

blocks.title: Deliverable-based retainers
blocks.text: If your retainer counts deliverables, such as 12 posts, rather than hours, the same method works. Track deliverables and revision rounds used against those included, and still log hours privately so you know your real effective rate for each client.

blocks.title: Small favours still count
blocks.text: It is fine to do a five-minute favour for a good client, but log it and mention it: 'We added the extra caption at no charge this time.' The client sees your goodwill, and you keep a record if favours start to grow.

takeaways: Effective hourly rate equals the monthly fee divided by the hours included.
Project the month-end hours at mid-month so you can act before an overrun.
New deliverables, extra revision rounds and rush work are change requests.
Answer extra requests with an estimate and clear options, confirmed in writing.

activity.title: Audit one retainer
steps: Write down the monthly fee and hours (or deliverables) included for one client.
Calculate your effective hourly rate.
Total the hours you actually spent last month and calculate your real hourly rate (fee divided by actual hours).
List any work you did that was outside the contract scope.
Draft a change request email for one of those items with an estimate and three options.
activity.evidence: A short sheet with the rate calculations, the list of out-of-scope work and your draft change request email

lessons.title: Running a quarterly business review that proves your value
objectives: Explain the purpose of a quarterly business review (QBR)
Prepare a results summary that compares outcomes with agreed goals
Present results honestly, separating what you caused from what you contributed to
Run a 60-minute QBR agenda and agree next-quarter goals

blocks.text: Weekly updates show activity. A **quarterly business review (QBR)** steps back to answer the questions a sponsor really asks: Are we getting results for our money? What did we learn? What should we do next? It is held every three months with your main contact and the sponsor. Done well, it is the single strongest tool for renewal, because the client hears your value from you before they hear a cheaper offer from someone else.

blocks.name: presentation
blocks.alt: A woman presenting results on a screen to colleagues
blocks.caption: A QBR is a short, honest presentation of results against the goals agreed at kickoff.

blocks.text: Prepare the results summary

Go back to the goals agreed at kickoff and report against them, not against whatever looks good. Use the client's own data where possible, such as orders from their sales records. Show the goal, the actual result and the difference. Then add two or three lessons learned and the risks you see coming.

blocks.title: Worked example: a bakery's online orders
blocks.context: For example, Ada's agency runs online marketing for a bakery in Port Harcourt on a N450,000 monthly retainer. The goal agreed at kickoff was 600 online orders in the quarter. The bakery's own order records are used. These are example figures.
steps: Actual online orders: 690. Against the goal: 690 divided by 600 = 1.15, so 115% of target.
Average order value from the bakery's records: N8,500. Online order revenue: 690 x 8,500 = N5,865,000.
Agency fees for the quarter: 3 x 450,000 = N1,350,000.
Revenue from online orders is about 5,865,000 divided by 1,350,000 = 4.3 times the fee.
Ada adds an honest note: some of these orders would have come anyway from loyal customers, so the agency contributed to this revenue but did not cause all of it.
blocks.result: The bakery owner sees clear progress against the agreed goal and trusts the numbers more because Ada did not claim credit for every naira. They agree a new goal of 750 orders for next quarter.

blocks.title: Never inflate results
blocks.text: Do not present guesses as facts, hide a missed target, or claim all of a client's growth. If a target was missed, say so, explain why and present your plan. Sponsors often check numbers, and one inflated claim can undo a year of trust.
A 60-minute agenda

head: Time
Section
What happens
rows: 5 min
Welcome and purpose
Thank them, confirm the agenda and who is present
15 min
Results against goals
Goal, actual, difference for each agreed measure
10 min
What we learned
What worked, what did not, and what you will change
15 min
Their priorities
Ask about changes in their business, budget and plans
10 min
Next quarter plan
Agree two or three goals and any change in scope
5 min
Close
Confirm actions, owners and the next QBR date

blocks.title: The quarterly review cycle
blocks.caption: Each QBR closes one quarter and sets the goals the next one will be judged against.

blocks.text: Listen more than you present

Give the client's priorities as much time as your results. Ask open questions such as: 'What has changed in your business since we last met?', 'What will your board or owner judge you on this year?' and 'What would make the next quarter a success for you personally?' Their answers feed the renewal and growth conversations in Module 3. Write them down in their own words.
Choosing the right measures

Report two kinds of measures. **Outcome measures** show what the client cares about, such as orders, enquiries, enrolments or money saved. **Activity measures** show what you did, such as posts published or reports filed. Lead with outcomes, because the sponsor is paying for results, and use activity measures to explain them. Choose no more than five measures in total, and keep the same ones each quarter so the client can compare.
When results are poor

Do not cancel or delay a QBR because the numbers are weak. A review held in a bad quarter often builds more trust than one held in a good quarter, because the client sees you face the facts. Show the shortfall, give your honest analysis of the causes, separate causes you control from those you do not, and bring a specific recovery plan with dates. Ask the client what they think went wrong; they often know things you do not.

blocks.title: Keep a goals register
blocks.text: Keep one page per client listing every goal agreed at kickoff and each QBR, with dates. It stops goals from quietly changing and makes the next review quick to prepare.

items: Send a short pre-read two days before, so the meeting is for discussion, not reading slides.
Keep the slides or document to about five pages; a phone-friendly PDF works well.
Send written notes with goals, actions and owners within one working day.

takeaways: A QBR reports results against the goals agreed at kickoff, using the client's data where possible.
Show goal, actual and difference, then lessons and risks.
Separate what you caused from what you contributed to; never inflate.
Spend as much time on the client's priorities as on your own results.

activity.title: Prepare a QBR pack
steps: Choose one client and write the two or three goals you agreed for the last quarter.
Collect the actual results and calculate the difference from each goal.
Write two lessons learned and one risk for next quarter.
Draft three open questions about the client's priorities.
Lay this out as a five-page pack using the 60-minute agenda.
activity.evidence: Your QBR pack (document or PDF) with goals, results, calculations, lessons and questions

quiz.q: A retainer pays N360,000 a month for 24 hours of work. What is the effective hourly rate?
On day 10 of a 30-day month, Chioma has used 12 of 30 retainer hours. If she continues at the same pace, how many hours will she use this month?
quiz.explain: 12 hours divided by 10 days, times 30 days = 36 hours, which is 6 hours over the retainer.

quiz.q: In a RACI chart, what is the common rule for the Accountable role?
options: There should be exactly one Accountable person per task
quiz.explain: One Accountable person per task gives a single clear decision-maker and avoids conflict.

quiz.q: A client asks for a short promotional video, which is not in the retainer. What should the account manager do first?
options: Do it quietly to keep the client happy
Log it, estimate hours and cost, and offer clear options in writing
Add the cost to next month's invoice without telling the client
quiz.explain: A change request should be logged, estimated and presented with choices so the client decides and the decision is recorded.

quiz.q: Sales grew 30% during your campaign quarter, but the client also opened a new branch. How should you report it at the QBR?
options: Claim the full 30% as your result
Report the growth, explain that the new branch also contributed, and show the measures your work directly affected
Say the growth was due to luck
quiz.explain: Honest reporting separates what you caused from what you contributed to, which makes the client trust all your numbers more.

quiz.q: Which item belongs in a communication charter?
options: Agreed response times and the escalation path
quiz.explain: A communication charter covers channels, response times, update days, approvals and escalation.

modules.title: Difficult Moments, Renewal and Your Client Playbook
modules.overview: Strong accounts are tested when something goes wrong, when a contract comes up for renewal, and when the person managing it changes. This module covers service recovery conversations, renewal and fair price adjustments, measuring growth across your client base, and the handover and reflection that complete your Client Relationship Management Playbook.

lessons.title: Delivering bad news and recovering from service failures
objectives: Prepare for a difficult client conversation using facts, impact and options
Deliver bad news early, by voice, and take clear ownership
Decide a fair, proportionate remedy and calculate its cost
Respond professionally when a client is angry or when the client is at fault

blocks.text: Every long client relationship includes failures: a missed deadline, a wrong figure in a report, a post that offended customers. Clients usually forgive a mistake. What they find hard to forgive is hearing about it late, hearing excuses, or discovering it themselves. How you handle a failure can leave the relationship weaker or, surprisingly often, stronger than before.

blocks.name: business-call
blocks.alt: A professional on a phone call at her desk
blocks.caption: Serious bad news belongs in a call, not a text message, followed by a written summary.

blocks.text: Before the conversation

items: Facts: what happened, when, and what is affected. Check them twice.
Cause: your honest understanding of why it happened, without blaming staff by name.
Impact on the client: what this means for their business, customers or reputation.
Options: two or three ways forward, with your recommendation.
Remedy: what you will do to make it right and to stop it happening again.

blocks.title: A service recovery conversation
blocks.caption: Speed and ownership come first; options and the written follow-up turn an apology into a plan.

blocks.text: During the conversation

Call as soon as you know, even before you have every answer. Open plainly: 'I need to tell you about a problem with the admissions campaign. It is our mistake.' Avoid long explanations at the start; the client wants to know what happened and what it means. Then listen. Let the client react without interrupting or defending. Summarise what you heard, present your options, agree the next step and say when you will update them again. Within the same day, send an email confirming what was agreed.

blocks.title: Worked example: a late campaign launch
blocks.context: For example, Ada's agency promised to launch a school's admissions campaign on 1 March. A design error meant it went live five days late. The school pays a N450,000 monthly retainer at an effective rate of N15,000 per hour. These are example figures.
steps: Ada calls the head of admissions on the morning she learns of the delay, not after launch.
She owns it: 'We did not check the final design in time. That is our failure.' She explains the impact: five fewer days of enquiries before the open day.
She offers options: (1) extend the campaign by five days at no cost; (2) add a free reminder post series in the week before the open day.
She proposes a remedy: four hours of extra work at no charge, worth 4 x 15,000 = N60,000.
She checks proportion: 60,000 divided by 450,000 = 0.133, about 13% of one month's fee, a meaningful gesture that the agency can afford.
She explains the prevention step: a second person now checks every final design two days before launch.
blocks.result: The school accepts the extension and the extra posts. At the next quarterly review, the head of admissions mentions that the agency's honesty about the delay was a reason to keep working together.

blocks.title: Remedies should fit the harm
blocks.text: A remedy is not a bribe. Offer something proportionate that repairs the actual damage, such as extra work or extended time, rather than a large discount that teaches the client to expect money every time something goes wrong. Never promise a remedy you cannot deliver.
When the client is angry

Stay calm and lower your voice rather than raising it. Acknowledge the feeling without accepting false facts: 'I can hear how frustrating this is.' Ask for time if you need to check something: 'Let me confirm the dates and call you back by 2pm.' If the client becomes abusive or threatening, you may end the call politely, write down what happened and involve your manager or the client's senior contact. Professional does not mean accepting abuse.
When the client is at fault

Sometimes the delay is theirs: approvals took a week, or content arrived late. Do not blame, but do not take the blame either. Point to the agreement calmly: 'Our charter allows two working days for approvals. The posts were approved on day six, so the launch moves to the 12th. Would you like us to prioritise anything to help?' This is why the communication charter and RACI chart from Module 2 matter: they turn arguments into facts.

items: After any failure, hold a short internal review within a week: what happened, why, and what process change prevents it.
Record the failure and the remedy in the client's file so the next account lead knows the history.
Check the account's health score the following month to see whether trust has recovered.

blocks.title: Data mistakes are serious
blocks.text: If a failure involves personal data, such as a customer list sent to the wrong person, tell the client immediately so they can meet their own legal duties. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets obligations for handling personal data and for responding to breaches.

takeaways: Tell the client early, by voice, and own the mistake in plain words.
Prepare facts, impact, options and a remedy before you call.
Make remedies proportionate to the harm and follow up in writing.
When the client is at fault, refer calmly to the agreed charter rather than blaming.

activity.title: Script a recovery call
steps: Choose a real past problem with a client, or a realistic one for your type of work.
Write the facts, cause, impact, two options and one proportionate remedy.
Calculate the cost of the remedy and its percentage of one month's fee.
Write the first three sentences you would say on the call.
Draft the follow-up email confirming what was agreed.
activity.evidence: Your recovery script with the remedy calculation and follow-up email

lessons.title: Renewals, fair price adjustments and measuring account growth
objectives: Plan a renewal timeline that starts 90 days before a contract ends
Calculate and justify a price adjustment and its yearly effect
Propose expansion only when it serves a goal the client has stated
Calculate net revenue retention for your client base

blocks.text: Many service providers treat renewal as paperwork that happens in the last week of a contract. By then it is too late to fix problems, the client's budget for next year may already be set, and a competitor may have been talking to them for months. Advanced account managers treat renewal as a planned process that starts well before the end date.

blocks.name: contract-signed
blocks.alt: A signed contract with a check mark
blocks.caption: A renewal is earned through the year and confirmed on paper at the end.

blocks.title: Renewal timeline
blocks.caption: Starting at 90 days leaves time to fix issues and fit the client's budget cycle.

blocks.text: Preparing the renewal conversation

At 90 days, look at the account's health score history, the QBR notes and the hours log. Ask yourself honestly: did we meet the goals, is this account profitable, and what does the client want next year? At 60 days, have a direct conversation: 'Our agreement ends on 31 December. Before I prepare a proposal, I would like to understand your plans for next year and anything you would like us to change.' Clients expect this conversation; avoiding it can look like you are unsure of your value.
Adjusting your price fairly

Your costs rise over time: data, fuel for generators, staff salaries, software subscriptions. If you never adjust prices, your profit on long accounts shrinks each year. A fair adjustment is explained with reasons, given with notice, and linked to value. Base the size of your adjustment on your actual cost increases and the results delivered, not on a figure copied from elsewhere.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 12% retainer adjustment
blocks.context: For example, Halima's school retainer is N450,000 a month. Her data, power and staff costs for this account have risen over the year, and the school met its enquiry goals. She proposes a 12% adjustment at renewal. These are example figures.
steps: New monthly fee: 450,000 x 1.12 = N504,000.
Old yearly value: 450,000 x 12 = N5,400,000. New yearly value: 504,000 x 12 = N6,048,000.
Yearly difference: 6,048,000 minus 5,400,000 = N648,000.
She writes the reasons in the proposal: rising delivery costs, goals met, and one added service (a monthly parents' newsletter) that the school asked for at the QBR.
She offers a choice: the full service at N504,000, or the current scope without the newsletter at a smaller adjustment.
blocks.result: The school chooses the full service. Because Halima raised the subject at 60 days with clear reasons and a choice, the bursar could fit it into next year's budget.

blocks.text: Expansion that serves the client

**Expansion** means a client buying more from you: more hours, a new service or a new branch. Good expansion starts from something the client said, usually at a QBR: 'We are opening a second branch in June' or 'Our parents complain they never hear from us.' Link your proposal to that statement in their words. If you cannot connect an offer to a stated goal, it is probably self-oriented selling, which lowers trust.
Measuring growth across all clients

**Net revenue retention (NRR)** shows whether your existing clients, taken together, are paying you more or less than a year ago. It ignores new clients, so it measures account management, not sales. Formula: (starting monthly revenue + expansion minus reductions minus lost clients) divided by starting monthly revenue, times 100. Above 100% means your existing accounts grew overall.

head: Item (monthly, example)
Amount
rows: Starting monthly revenue from existing clients
Expansion: Client B added a service
Reduction: Client D cut its scope
minus N50,000
Lost: Client E did not renew
minus N100,000
Result: 1,400,000 divided by 1,300,000
about 107.7%

blocks.text: When the client pushes back

Some clients will ask you to keep the old price or to cut it. Listen first and ask why: a tight budget, a cheaper quote, or doubt about value each need a different answer. If the budget is tight, offer a smaller scope at a fair price rather than the same work for less, because discounting the same work lowers your effective hourly rate for the whole year. If they have a cheaper quote, remind them of the results in your QBR and the cost of switching, without criticising the competitor. If they doubt the value, that is a warning sign you missed earlier; agree clear goals for the next quarter. Know in advance the lowest fee at which the account is still worth keeping.

blocks.title: Read NRR with your health scores
blocks.text: An NRR above 100% can still hide risk if most growth came from one client. Check concentration from Module 1 at the same time.

takeaways: Start renewal work 90 days before the contract ends.
Justify price adjustments with real cost changes and results, give notice and offer choices.
Propose expansion only when it links to a goal the client has stated.
Net revenue retention above 100% means existing clients grew overall.

activity.title: Plan one renewal
steps: Pick a client whose contract ends in the next six months and write the dates for the 90, 60, 45 and 30-day steps.
List your actual cost increases for this account over the last year.
Calculate a proposed new fee, the new yearly value and the yearly difference.
Write one expansion idea linked to something the client said, quoting their words.
Calculate NRR for your client base over the last 12 months.
activity.evidence: A renewal plan page with dates, price calculations, one expansion idea and your NRR calculation

lessons.title: Account handover, honest reflection and your client playbook
objectives: Write a handover note that lets a colleague take over an account without losing trust
Plan a joint introduction and an overlap period for a handover
Write an honest reflection on a relationship challenge using the STAR structure
Assemble the three parts of your Client Relationship Management Playbook

blocks.text: Accounts are often lost at the moment the account manager changes. The new person does not know the history, repeats questions the client has answered many times, and misses promises made by the last person. Whether you are leaving a role, going on maternity leave or giving an account to a team member as you grow, a planned handover protects the client and your reputation.

blocks.name: reviewed-docs
blocks.alt: A stack of checked documents ready to hand over
blocks.caption: A complete handover file means the client never has to explain their history twice.

blocks.text: What goes in a handover note

blocks.title: Account handover checklist
blocks.caption: Tick every item before the outgoing manager steps away from the account.

blocks.text: Write the note so a capable stranger could run the account tomorrow. Include the client's goals in their own words, sensitive topics to handle carefully (for example, a past dispute that was resolved), the communication charter, the last QBR notes and any change requests in progress. Transfer platform access by adding the new person's own login and removing the old one; never pass passwords along in a WhatsApp message.

blocks.title: Worked example: handing over three accounts
blocks.context: For example, Ada's senior account manager, Kemi, is leaving after giving a month's notice. Kemi manages Clients A, B and C, worth N600,000, N250,000 and N200,000 a month. These are example figures.
steps: Because Client A is strategic and amber on its health score, Ada takes it herself; Tolu takes B and C.
Kemi writes one handover note per client using the checklist, and Ada reviews each one within two days.
In week 2, Kemi and the new lead hold a joint call with each client. Kemi introduces the new lead and confirms every open promise.
For the next two weeks the new lead runs the account while Kemi is still available for questions; after that, Kemi's access is removed.
blocks.result: All three clients renew at year end. Client A's sponsor later says the joint call made the change feel planned rather than sudden.

blocks.text: Reflecting honestly on a challenge

Employers and clients are more impressed by honest reflection on a hard situation than by stories where everything went perfectly. Use the **STAR** structure: **Situation** (the context), **Task** (what you were responsible for), **Action** (what you actually did) and **Result** (what happened, with numbers where possible). Then add a fifth part: **what I would do differently**. Remove client names and any confidential details, or ask permission before sharing.

head: STAR part
Example notes
rows: Situation
A school client's new bursar questioned our retainer two months before renewal
Task
As account lead, I had to keep the account and rebuild trust with the new decision-maker
Action
I requested a meeting, prepared a QBR with goals and results, and listened to her concerns about reporting
Result
The school renewed with a simpler monthly report; the account health score rose from 3.1 to 4.0 over two quarters
Do differently
Meet any new decision-maker within the first two weeks, not wait for them to raise concerns

blocks.text: Your Client Relationship Management Playbook

Your capstone brings this course together into a playbook you can reuse with every important client. It has three parts: an onboarding communication template (kickoff agenda, communication charter and RACI from Module 2), a documented relationship challenge (your STAR reflection, plus the recovery script from Lesson 1 of this module if relevant) and a proactive check-in and renewal plan (health score routine, QBR dates, renewal timeline and feedback questions).
When you receive an account

If you are the person taking over, read everything before you speak to the client: the contract, the charter, the last three reports, the QBR notes and the health score history. In your first call, do not ask questions the client has already answered in writing. Instead say what you understand and ask them to correct you: 'I understand your main goal this year is the second branch launch in June. Is that still right?' Keep every promise the previous manager made, even small ones, or explain clearly and early if one cannot be kept.

items: Read the full file before the first call.
Confirm goals and open promises in your own words.
Send a short note after the call listing what you will do and by when.

blocks.title: Tell clients early
blocks.text: Tell important clients about a change of account manager as soon as the decision is final, ideally before the outgoing person announces it elsewhere.

blocks.title: Keep it alive
blocks.text: Review the playbook every quarter. Add what you learn from each QBR, renewal and difficult moment, so it becomes your own working method rather than a document you wrote once.

takeaways: A planned handover with a joint introduction protects accounts when people change.
Never pass passwords on; give new people their own access and remove old access.
STAR plus 'what I would do differently' makes an honest, credible reflection.
Your playbook combines onboarding, a documented challenge and a renewal plan.

activity.title: Draft a handover note and a STAR reflection
steps: Choose one account and write a handover note covering every checklist item.
Mark any open promises with their due dates.
Write a STAR reflection on a real relationship challenge, with the fifth part 'what I would do differently'.
Remove or disguise client names and confidential details.
activity.evidence: A handover note and a one-page STAR reflection, ready for your playbook

quiz.q: Bola discovers on Monday that a report she promised for Wednesday will be two days late. What should she do?
options: Wait until Wednesday in case she finishes
Call the client on Monday, own the delay, explain the impact and offer options
Send a short text on Thursday
quiz.explain: Early, spoken, honest news with options protects trust far better than waiting or blaming.

quiz.q: A retainer of N300,000 a month is adjusted by 10% at renewal. What is the yearly difference in fees?
quiz.explain: New fee is 300,000 x 1.10 = N330,000. The monthly difference is N30,000, and 30,000 x 12 = N360,000 a year.

quiz.q: Starting monthly revenue from existing clients is N1,000,000. Expansion adds N100,000, reductions remove N50,000 and a lost client removes N150,000. What is the net revenue retention?
When should renewal work normally begin for a 12-month contract?
options: On the last day of the contract
quiz.explain: Starting about 90 days before leaves time to fix problems, discuss plans and fit the client's budget cycle.

quiz.q: Approvals from a client took six working days, although the charter allows two, so the launch is late. What is the best response?
options: Take all the blame to keep the peace
Tell the client their team is careless
Calmly refer to the charter, give the new date and offer help with priorities
quiz.explain: Pointing calmly to the agreed charter states the facts without blame and keeps the relationship professional.

quiz.q: Which is the safest way to give a new account manager access to a client's social media accounts?
options: Add the new person with their own login and remove the old person's access
Write the password in the handover note
quiz.explain: Personal logins can be tracked and removed, which protects the client's accounts and data.

finalQuiz.q: A business earns N2,000,000 a month, of which one client pays N900,000. What is that client's share?
finalQuiz.explain: 900,000 divided by 2,000,000 = 0.45, so 45%, a high concentration risk.

finalQuiz.q: Which part of the Trust Equation rises when a provider keeps pitching new services the client never asked for?
finalQuiz.explain: Constant selling shows focus on yourself. Self-orientation is the denominator, so trust falls.

finalQuiz.q: Health score weights are 25%, 15%, 25%, 20% and 15%. A client scores 5, 5, 4, 4, 3. What is the total?
What is the main purpose of a communication charter?
options: To agree channels, response times, updates and escalation with the client
finalQuiz.explain: The charter sets the agreed rules for how both sides communicate, protecting the client's expectations and your time.

finalQuiz.q: In a RACI chart for approving health information posts, who should be Accountable?
options: The client's senior person qualified to approve health content
finalQuiz.explain: One accountable decision-maker per task; for health information, it should be the client's qualified senior person.

finalQuiz.q: A retainer is N600,000 for 40 hours. A change request is estimated at 6 hours. What should it cost at the retainer rate?
finalQuiz.explain: The rate is 600,000 divided by 40 = N15,000 per hour, and 6 x 15,000 = N90,000.

finalQuiz.q: At 75% of retainer hours used in a month, what should the account manager do?
options: Tell the client and agree priorities for the rest of the month
Keep working and invoice later without notice
finalQuiz.explain: Raising it early lets the client choose priorities and avoids a surprise overrun.

finalQuiz.q: At a QBR, the client's orders beat the goal, but a holiday season also boosted sales. What is the best way to present this?
options: Report the result against the goal and note that the season also contributed
Hide the season from the client
finalQuiz.explain: Separating your contribution from outside factors keeps your reporting credible.

finalQuiz.q: Which remedy is most proportionate for a five-day campaign delay on a N450,000 monthly retainer?
options: Extend the campaign and add a few hours of free work
Promise free work for a year
finalQuiz.explain: A remedy should repair the actual harm and be affordable; extending the campaign with a small amount of free work does that.

finalQuiz.q: Why should renewal conversations start about 60 to 90 days before a contract ends?
options: To leave time to fix issues and fit the client's budget planning
finalQuiz.explain: Early renewal work gives time to address concerns and to fit next year's budget.

finalQuiz.q: Starting monthly revenue is N800,000. Expansion is N200,000, reductions N0, and lost clients N100,000. What is net revenue retention?
An account manager is leaving. Which step best protects the client relationship?
options: Email the client the new manager's name on the last day
Hold a joint introduction call and confirm all open promises before access is switched
Share the old manager's passwords with the new one
Pause the account for a month
finalQuiz.explain: A joint call and a written handover of open promises make the change feel planned and keep commitments visible.

capstone.title: Client Relationship Management Playbook
capstone.brief: Produce a reusable playbook for managing one real or realistic high-value client, made of three parts: an onboarding communication template that sets scope, communication and issue-handling expectations; a documented example of a real relationship challenge with honest STAR reflection; and a plan for proactive check-ins, feedback and renewal.
steps: Choose one current or realistic high-value client and record its monthly value, share of your income and tier.
Part 1: write the kickoff agenda, a one-page communication charter and a RACI chart for four recurring tasks.
Part 2: document one real relationship challenge using STAR plus 'what I would do differently', and add a recovery script if the challenge involved a service failure.
Part 3: set up the monthly health score for the account, schedule the next four QBR dates, and write the 90, 60, 45 and 30-day renewal steps with three feedback questions you will ask.
Add your renewal price calculation and one expansion idea linked to a goal the client has stated.
Remove or disguise confidential client details, then review the playbook with a peer or mentor and make one improvement.
evidence: Client value, income share and tier calculation
Kickoff agenda, communication charter and RACI chart with one Accountable per task
STAR reflection on a real challenge, including what you would do differently
Health score sheet with at least one completed month
Calendar of QBR dates and renewal steps with feedback questions
Renewal price calculation and one expansion idea quoting the client's stated goal
